newsitem.title: USA: Union leader sees Clinton drifting from labor.
newsitem.headline: Union leader sees Clinton drifting from labor.

text.p: The leader of the country's largest public sector labor union Thursday said President Clinton appeared to be moving away from labor on several key issues of importance to the labor movement.

Gerald McEntee, president of the 1.3 million member American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME), said the administration was drifting away from labor on issues such as Medicare, the federal budget, welfare reform and privatization of government services.
"We're concerned with the direction of the president and the administrationin a number of areas," said McEntee.
"We're more concerned over the fact that we thought that we played a part in his election victory," he told a group of reporters. "And now we see a change."

McEntee, who is also on the 54-member AFL-CIO Executive Council, was one of the architects behind organized labor's stepped-up political activism last year that included issue-oriented, hit-and-run television advertising blitzes that infuriated congressional Republicans.

His comments, coming ahead of AFSCME's biennial legislative conference next week, marked a departure from the generally unwavering public support for the administration that has come from the leadership of the 78-union American Federation of Labor-Congress of Industrial Organizations.

Key concerns include the extent to which the administration is willing to go to cut Medicare, other programs and capital gains taxes to reach a balanced budget deal with Republicans and a sense that White House officials are "negotiating with themselves, constantly retreating," he said.
"It would be better for Clinton to have no agreement than to have a bad agreement," McEntee said.

The debate over saving the government's financially troubled Medicare retiree health care system figured prominently in the elections and unions rallied their members around the plan for less drastic cuts staked out by Clinton.

Another concern, McEntee said, was the lack of training and preparation for some 2 million welfare receipients who could enter the workforce following last year's reform legislation, and whether they would have the legal status of workers.
Unions have been assured that the new workers would be covered by minimum wage and other federal labor protections.
"But we have yet to see it," he added.
